h1: Upgrading from a starter kit to full all-grain equipment
title: Upgrading a Starter Kit to All-Grain | Craft Beer School
desc: What to buy, in what order, when you move from a homebrew starter kit to all-grain brewing in India: kettle, heat, chiller, mash tun and temperature control.
teaser: You have outgrown the starter kit. Here is what to buy first, what can wait and the upgrade that improves beer most.
standfirst: Moving to all-grain is the point where homebrewing starts to look like real brewing. It is also where people overspend on shiny kit and underspend on the one thing that matters most. Here is the order we would buy in.
sections: Decide your batch size before anything else

Every piece of equipment follows from batch size. Most homebrewers settle on about 20 litres into the fermenter, which fills a standard fermenting bucket and gives two cases of bottles. Smaller batches of 10 litres suit a flat kitchen and let you brew more often. Bigger batches save little time and need a stronger back.

Pick a size and stick to it. A kettle bought for 10 litre batches is useless when you decide to brew 40.
Choose a system: bag, three vessels or all-in-one

There are three common routes.

  • Brew in a bag. One kettle, one fine mesh bag. You mash in the kettle, lift the grain out and boil. It is the cheapest and simplest step up. See our brew in a bag guide for the method.
  • Three vessels. A hot water tank, a mash tun and a kettle. More kit and more space, but full control over sparging. Many people build the mash tun from an insulated cooler box with a false bottom.
  • All-in-one electric. A single vessel with a built-in element, pump and grain basket. Tidy and repeatable, but the most expensive.

For a first all-grain setup in an Indian flat, brew in a bag is hard to beat. You can add a mash tun later without wasting the kettle.
The kettle and the heat source

For 20 litre batches by brew in a bag, the kettle must hold the full volume of water plus grain, so aim for 40 litres or more. For a three vessel system, 35 litres is enough. Buy stainless steel with a ball valve fitted near the base. Aluminium works, but stainless is easier to clean and lasts.

Heat is where Indian homes complicate things. A strong LPG burner gets 25 litres to a boil quickly, but it belongs on a balcony or terrace with good airflow, never in a closed kitchen. An electric element is cleaner indoors. A 3 kW element on a standard 230 V supply draws about 13 amps, so it needs a 16 amp socket on a circuit that can carry it. Check with an electrician before you plug it in. A lesser element will still boil, just slowly.

A wort chiller is the upgrade beginners skip and regret. Cooling 20 litres from boiling to pitching temperature in an ice bath takes an hour or more. A copper or stainless immersion chiller connected to a tap does it in 20 to 30 minutes, which cuts the time the wort sits warm and exposed.

In summer, tap and borewell water in much of India runs at 25 to 30 °C, so a chiller alone cannot reach an ale pitching temperature of 18 to 20 °C. The usual trick is to run tap water until the wort is near 35 °C, then pump iced water through the coil for the last stretch.
Temperature control is the biggest single upgrade

If we could give a homebrewer one piece of kit, it would not be a fancy kettle. It would be a fermentation chamber: an old fridge or chest freezer with an inexpensive external temperature controller.

Yeast makes most of the flavour in beer and it is very sensitive to temperature. An ale fermenting at 28 °C in a Chennai flat will throw off fruity esters and harsh fusel alcohols no matter how good the recipe. Held at 18 °C, the same wort makes clean beer. A controller that switches the fridge on and off around a probe taped to the fermenter is the cheapest way to fix a hot climate. It also opens the door to lagers.

A grain mill can wait while you have a supplier who crushes malt for you. A pump can wait while gravity and a jug do the job. A refractometer can wait while your hydrometer works. Kegging is lovely, but bottles still make good beer.

Buy in this order: kettle and heat source, chiller, fermentation temperature control, then a mash tun or mill. Each step should fix a problem you have actually had, not one you read about.

Better equipment gives you control. It does not tell you what to do with it. People who spend serious money on kit and still brew thin, sweet or cidery beer usually have a process gap rather than an equipment gap. If you are ready for your first all-grain brew day and want someone to explain the why behind each step, that is the gap we teach to close.
faqs: What size kettle do I need for all-grain brewing?
For 20 litre batches, about 40 litres if you brew in a bag, since the kettle holds the water and the grain. A three vessel system can use a 35 litre kettle.
Is brew in a bag real all-grain brewing?
Yes. You mash crushed malt and convert its starch to sugar, which is what all-grain means. Many good homebrewers use nothing else.
What is the best first upgrade for homebrewing in India?
Fermentation temperature control. A fridge or freezer with an external controller lets yeast work at the right temperature, which improves flavour more than any kettle.
Can I use an electric element on Indian household power?
Often yes, but a 3 kW element draws about 13 amps at 230 V. It needs a 16 amp socket on a suitable circuit, so check with an electrician first.
